steps.label: Do Now: Character Sets
steps.content:
Do Now: Character Sets

Quick recap from last lesson before today's challenges start.

options: A list of every key on the keyboard
A set of characters where each one has been given a unique binary code
A font style used to display text
items.explain: A character set assigns every character - letters, digits, symbols - a unique binary code, so a computer can store and display text.

items.prompt: Why is Unicode needed as well as ASCII?
options: ASCII does not include enough characters for every language and symbol used around the world
ASCII stopped working and had to be replaced
items.explain: ASCII only covers a few hundred characters at most - nowhere near enough for every language, emoji and symbol in use worldwide, which is exactly what Unicode was built for.

steps.label: Pixel Lab
steps.content:
Data Representation

Pixel Lab

Year 10, 1.2 L2 · Images · 30 minutes

  • Challenge 1: Watch a picture appear from raw hex bytes, one row at a time.
  • Challenge 2: Decode a hidden bitmap yourself.
  • Challenge 3: Drag a resolution slider and watch a real photo - and its file size - change live.
  • Challenge 4: Do the same with colour depth.
  • Challenge 5: Design your own pixel art, first in black and white, then in colour.

steps.label: Challenge 1: Bytes Become a Picture
steps.content:
Challenge 1: Bytes Become a Picture

This is an actual (simplified) bitmap file. Press Step forward, or Play all, and watch each hex byte turn into a row of real pixels on the left - at the exact same moment.

steps.label: Challenge 2: Decode a Bitmap
steps.content:
Challenge 2: Decode a Bitmap Yourself

Now you do it by hand. Read each row of stored pixel data from left to right. Click a square when the bit is 1. Leave it white when the bit is 0.

steps.label: Challenge 3: Resolution Live
steps.content:
Challenge 3: Resolution, Live

Resolution is the number of pixels used to make up an image (width x height). Drag the slider from low to high. Watch the picture, and the file size underneath it, change in real time.

Find the lowest resolution where you can still tell what the picture is.

steps.label: Challenge 4: Colour Depth Live
steps.content:
Challenge 4: Colour Depth, Live

Colour depth is the number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel. Possible colours = 2depth. Drag the slider and watch the same picture - and its file size - change.

Find the lowest colour depth before the picture starts to look wrong (banding, blotchy colours).

steps.label: Challenge 5: Pixel Art in Black and White
steps.content:
Challenge 5: Pixel Art in Black and White

A 1-bit image can only use 2 colours. Design a simple 10 x 10 pixel picture (a face, a heart, an icon) using only black and white.

steps.label: Challenge 6: Pixel Art in Colour
steps.content:
Challenge 6: Pixel Art in Colour

A 2-bit image can use 4 colours. Try the same picture again, or a new one - notice how much more you can show with just 2 more colours.

steps.label: Challenge 7: Free Play
steps.content:
Challenge 7: Free Play

Both sliders are unlocked. Image data in bits = width x height x colour depth. Try to get the smallest possible file size where the picture is still recognisable.

y10_1_2_l2_practice.feedback: Valid metadata includes the width, the height (or resolution), or the colour depth.

y10_1_2_l2_plenary.feedback: A pixel is the smallest individual point of colour in a bitmap image.
Image resolution is the number of pixels used to represent the image, usually written as width x height.
Increasing colour depth allows more colours (smoother, more realistic images) and increases the amount of data stored.
